claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 typically contains residual porosity.
Grain-boundary defects and residual pores in conventional ZrB2 are vulnerable to liquid intrusion during plating.
SPS can densify single-phase ZrB2 near 2000 °C rather than above 2300 °C.
SPS uses rapid heating, pulsed electric current, and applied mechanical pressure to enhance consolidation.
The proposed SPS preparation uses an inert or vacuum atmosphere, a temperature near 2000 °C, pressure on the order of 50 MPa, and rapid heating.
SPS processing will produce a more coherently densified ZrB2 microstructure with less residual porosity.
SPS processing will reduce the number of defective grain boundaries in ZrB2.
Pulsed electric current and mechanical pressure in SPS induce localized heating and enhanced diffusion at particle contacts.
Localized heating and enhanced contact diffusion accelerate ZrB2 densification at lower temperatures than conventional sintering.
Rapid SPS densification limits grain growth and pore formation.
A denser microstructure restricts penetration of the liquid plating bath.
Restricting plating-liquid penetration reduces the formation of holes that can cause component failure.
Compared with ZrB2 conventionally sintered at or above 2300 °C, ZrB2 SPS-processed near 2000 °C will have lower porosity.
Compared with conventionally sintered ZrB2, SPS-processed ZrB2 will have higher mechanical strength.
Compared with conventionally sintered ZrB2, SPS-processed ZrB2 will develop fewer or smaller holes during prolonged plating-bath exposure.
The predicted benefit is limited to optimized SPS parameters and plating-bath chemistries and exposure conditions within the studied range.
The magnitude of temperature reduction, strength improvement, and hole resistance may depend on SPS optimization and industrial component scale.
